item.title: "Passive" Versus “Global Workspace” Views of Consciousness
item.description:
Consciousness

"Passive" Versus “Global Workspace” Views of Consciousness

Both views state that consciousness integrates things, but they differ in ways.

Posted March 11, 2026

Key points
  • Both "passive" and "global workspace" views of consciousness propose that consciousness integrates things.
  • However, the two accounts differ in several important ways.
  • Global workspace accounts propose that consciousness carries out many functions, including decision-making.
  • Passive views propose that consciousness does one thing: Present contents to (unconscious) action systems.

In “passive” theoretical accounts of consciousness, the conscious field, which is composed of everything one is aware of at one moment in time, can be conceptualized as a static structure. In this way, the field resembles any mental representation of any bit of knowledge. Decision-making, deliberating, and “action selection” (in which one decides what to do) are carried out at stages of processing subsequent to that of the conscious field. In line with this view, the great theorists Karl Lashley, George Miller, and Roger Shepard proposed that one is conscious of the products of thinking, but not of the thinking itself. This idea has recurred in the histories of psychology and neuroscience.

A painting by Joan Miró that conveys the varied contents of the conscious field: Horse, Pipe and Red Flower (1920). Philadelphia Museum of Art.
Source: Wikipedia: Public Domain

Thus, from this standpoint, there are no decision-making or executive functions carried out by the conscious field. The conscious field is as passive as a car window or a television screen, simply presenting contents, such as percepts, urges, and memories, to response systems (which are unconscious). Regarding a television screen, one can change the channel, but the movie being played can’t do anything. This is how the field is: Figuratively speaking, it cannot do anything other than play the movie.

But this does not mean that the conscious field is unnecessary. In biology, there are many things that are passive but necessary, such as passive ion channels in the membranes of neurons. The conscious field is necessary for all the contents in consciousness (the sights, sounds, and memories) to influence collectively the (unconscious) action selection system. Much like a movie, the field is thus construed as a multidimensional structure (to convey the various sensory contents, urges, and memories) that differentially activates the many response systems (also called “response codes”).

Another painting by Joan Miró (The Tilled Field, 1923–1924) that conveys the medley of contents that can occupy the conscious field. Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.
Source: Wikipedia: Public Domain

What is meant by “static” and “passive”? Consider your mental representation that ravens are black. You cannot, at will, change this knowledge and pretend that you do not know that ravens are black. You can imagine a pink raven, but this will not remove your belief that ravens are actually black. The representation, as far as your voluntary processes are concerned, is static, unmodifiable, immutable, much like a toothache or nausea. Other things can affect these representations, but not your voluntary processes or executive functions. The representation (ravens are black) is experienced, but is much like a memory. Memories change on their own, but it is hard to change them at will. According to passive accounts, the conscious field is of this static nature.

This is in contrast to the influential and groundbreaking “global workspace” accounts of consciousness (e.g., Baars, 1988; Dehaene, 2014), in which consciousness does many things and permits cognitive content to be globally available to various cognitive processes. Unlike in passive accounts, things do happen in consciousness. The cognitive content in consciousness is “broadcast” to brain modules responsible both for the generation of conscious contents and the interpretation of conscious contents. Consciousness is responsible for functions such as decision-making, analogy forming, adaptation and learning, metacognitive self-monitoring, editing and debugging, and auto-programming (Baars, 1988).

In passive accounts, the only thing consciousness does is present all the activated contents at one moment in time (which is tricky) to the (unconscious) action systems. (The simultaneous presentation of contents is an achievement because sensory systems operate at different speeds.) From the passive point of view, a conscious content cannot cause the generation of any other conscious content. The field has only “one-way communication” with the action systems, systems which are unconscious. And the response systems do not need to “read” or “interpret” the configuration of the conscious field, as this would introduce a variation of the homunculus fallacy. Consider that, if the percepts and other contents of the conscious field are in fact “perceived” by the action systems, then the action systems, too, must have some kind of perceptual system. This would repeat the process of perception over and over, ad infinitum. Instead, the configuration of the conscious field at one moment in time directly causes the response systems to be differentially activated, and this determines what we do. No repeat of perception is necessary. The contents of the field wholly and exclusively determine what we do next (“action selection”). It is similar to the way that an audio speaker directly affects our eardrum.

It should be noted that, in both passive accounts and global workspace accounts, consciousness can bring together various types of contents (e.g., percepts, urges, and memories). The question now becomes, what physical thing can achieve this with the energy efficiency of the brain, which, unlike computers, requires no cooling fans and maintains a temperature only slightly above 98.6° F? See here for further discussion of this question.

item.title: Why Medical Challenges Can Feel So Lonely
item.description:
Loneliness

Why Medical Challenges Can Feel So Lonely

When health stress separates you from others, here’s how to close the gap.

Posted March 11, 2026

Key points
  • Health-related challenges can make us feel lonely—often because we feel unseen, not because we're truly alone.
  • Medical stress can disrupt identity, relationships, and sense of meaning.
  • Self-expression through writing, art, or movement can bridge inner and outer worlds.
  • Intentional connection (and knowing when to share or conserve energy) builds resilience.
Source: Resat Kuleli / Unsplash

Co-Authored by Nina Bakoyiannis, Ph.D., and Amy Vigliotti, Ph,D,

When facing health stressors, loneliness is a common, yet often invisible experience. Loneliness is rarely about being physically alone, but rather the sense of not being seen or understood by others. It can emerge even when surrounded by supportive friends and family, so long as we are left with the emotional experience of disconnection.

“Loneliness is not just the absence of people. It is the absence of purpose, the absence of meaning. When you find yourself in a world where everything seems alien and distant, where every connection is superficial, and every attempt at understanding is met with indifference, you realize that true loneliness is not being alone, but feeling alone in a world that no longer makes sense.”

This quote—from an unknown source, though social media accounts frequently attribute it to novelist Haruki Murakami—captures the layers of loneliness: There's a disconnection from ourselves, seen in a loss of purpose or meaning; there’s disconnection from others, as in feeling a distance; and there’s disconnection from the world, where interactions may feel superficial and the world around you no longer feels familiar.

For those experiencing medical challenges, this can feel especially salient. The world keeps moving, yet your internal experience has fundamentally shifted. There may exist what feels like a gap between who you were and where you are now.

Source: Chris Nagahama / Unsplash

Why Loneliness and Illness Go Hand in Hand

There are many reasons loneliness can emerge during a medical journey. Physical changes such as fatigue, pain, or limitations in daily activities can make it harder to engage. Relationships may feel different, as if others don’t fully understand or don’t know what to say.

Small role shifts at home, at work, or socially can create a subtle, but painful sense of distance. In addition, there is often the lingering emotional weight of uncertainty, vulnerability, and fear.

Practical steps can help, including:

  • Notice your loneliness. Start by recognizing when you feel isolated or disconnected. Pay attention to your body, thoughts, and emotional cues. Keeping a small journal or simply noting your feelings can help understand what triggers loneliness.
  • Build the capacity to be alone. Intentionally spend time in your own company. This could be a quiet walk, reading, or simply sitting with your thoughts. Learning to be comfortable alone can help you feel safer in your own mind. If loneliness is about the experience of not being known, we first need the capacity to know ourselves in order to share ourselves.
  • Build self-expression and inner strength. Expression bridges the gap between your inner world and the outside world. Try writing, art, music, or movement to give your thoughts and emotions a tangible form. It’s important to let go of comparison or self-judgment, and instead focus on what feels meaningful and authentic. Do it for yourself, not an audience.
  • Build connections. Even small steps can make a meaningful difference. This might include opening up to trusted friends or family, joining communities where others understand medical challenges firsthand, or giving back through volunteering or mentoring. Connection does not only have to be conversation; it can be any shared experience, creative pursuit, or contribution.
  • Manage discomfort and discern when to express. Part of navigating loneliness is tolerating the discomfort that comes with vulnerability. Connection, however, does not mean we must share everything with everyone. We are also allowed to choose intentionally.
  • Remember: You don't always have to share. Sometimes speaking up feels relieving and clarifying, but there may also be moments when conserving your energy, setting boundaries, or deciding not to explain yourself is protective. The goal is not constant openness, but thoughtful expression. Asking yourself, “What feels needed right now? Expression or containment?” can help guide that decision. Over time, this discernment strengthens both self-trust and relationships.

Loneliness during a medical journey is not a sign of weakness. It is a deeply human response to change, uncertainty, and disruption. By noticing it, strengthening your ability to be with yourself, expressing your inner world, connecting intentionally and discerning when and how to share, you can gradually move from feeling unseen toward feeling understood and grounded.

item.title: Quiet Is Not Weakness
item.description:
Adolescence

Quiet Is Not Weakness

What quiet adolescents teach us about strength.

Posted March 11, 2026

In classrooms, quiet adolescents are often the ones adults worry about most. Teachers may wonder whether they are disengaged, unsure of themselves, or struggling socially. Yet many quiet teenagers are not withdrawn from the world around them. They are paying close attention to it.

In clinical work, some of the most important aspects of development are easy to overlook. Not because they are hidden, but because they do not announce themselves. In this column, I reflect on the quieter moments in adolescent development that exist outside formal diagnoses and treatment plans. Some of the most meaningful forms of growth occur long before they become visible to others.

Quiet adolescents are often misunderstood. Their strengths do not announce themselves in the ways adults and institutions typically reward. In classrooms, social settings, and even families, silence can easily be interpreted as hesitation, disengagement, or uncertainty, when it often reflects careful observation, thoughtful processing, and deliberate engagement with the world.

In many environments, silence is quickly interpreted as the absence of confidence, engagement, or ability. A student who speaks less may be assumed to be unsure. A teenager who listens more than they talk may be viewed as withdrawn. Yet developmental research on social withdrawal in childhood and adolescence suggests that quiet behavior can reflect a range of developmental pathways and should not automatically be equated with disengagement or dysfunction.

The quiet adolescents in my life have taught me this slowly. One young person close to me rarely rushes to speak, but when she does, her words are careful and precise. Watching her move through the world has been a reminder of how easily quiet can be mistaken for uncertainty when it is often a form of attention. Some adolescents simply take time to understand what is happening around them before deciding how they wish to respond.

Differences in temperament are widely recognized in psychology, and some young people naturally approach unfamiliar situations with watchfulness before engagement. What may appear cautious on the surface can reflect attentiveness rather than avoidance. Some individuals also process sensory and emotional information more deeply, noticing subtleties in their environments and taking longer to integrate new experiences before responding.

Modern social environments frequently reward speed of expression and visibility of opinion. In classrooms, workplaces, and digital spaces, those who speak first and most often are often perceived as more confident or capable. Quick responses may be mistaken for clarity, while pauses may be interpreted as uncertainty.

Yet reflective processing and observational learning represent equally important ways of engaging with the world. Individuals who pause before responding often integrate information more deeply before speaking. They listen carefully, notice patterns, and consider implications before offering their perspective.

These differences often become particularly visible during adolescence. At this stage of development, young people are forming identity, testing possibilities, and gradually assembling a coherent sense of self. Some do this externally and aloud. Others do it through quieter forms of observation, reflection, and selective expression.

In clinical conversations with adolescents, these differences in temperament appear regularly. Some young people begin speaking about their experiences almost immediately, while others observe before entering the conversation. What initially appears as hesitation often reflects a young person taking time to orient themselves before expressing what they think or feel.

In many classrooms, the student who speaks the least is often the one teachers worry about most. Quiet participation can easily be mistaken for disengagement. Yet when such students are given time to respond without pressure, their answers often reveal a depth of understanding that had been developing quietly all along.

Confidence among quieter adolescents may not resemble the assertiveness often associated with leadership or participation. It may appear instead in the ability to tolerate uncertainty, to form independent perspectives without needing immediate affirmation, and to speak only when something meaningful feels ready to be expressed.

In a culture that frequently rewards performance and visibility, quieter forms of strength can remain hidden in plain sight. Listening, reflection, and careful observation contribute to learning, empathy, and insight in ways that are no less significant than more outward styles of participation.

Sometimes the most supportive thing an adult can do is notice who a young person is becoming and allow that process the time and space it requires. Development does not always unfold through visibility. Some of the most important forms of growth occur quietly long before they become visible to others.

Quiet adolescents are not necessarily searching for a voice. Many already have one. They are simply learning when it matters to use it. Development does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it appears in the young person who watches carefully, thinks deeply, and speaks only when something meaningful is ready to be said.

Read the original article on Psychology Today →

item.title: The Ethics of Dog-Human Relationships—The Trouble with Play
item.description:
Relationships

The Ethics of Dog-Human Relationships—The Trouble with Play

Julia B. Linares-Roake offers a unique view of play from the dogs' perspective.

Posted March 12, 2026

Key points
  • Focusing on defamiliarization, she asks us to step back from what we think play is supposed to offer.
  • She wonders if our relationships with dogs are always good for them as we over-control their lives.
  • In the United States, shelter dogs who don’t choose to play with objects are less likely to be adopted.
Source: Rebecca Niemiec/with permission.

Play behavior, whether it's by dogs, cats, other companion animals, or wild, freely roaming creatures, is a topic that attracts widespread transdisciplinary interest along with curiosity from people who love to watch animals at play or simply want to know more about this joy-filled activity.

When I first learned about the work of Dr. Julia B. Linares-Roake on her unique perspectives of dog-human play, in which she explores how people navigate the muddiness of living with their dogs through play, I couldn't wait for her to finish her research and find out more about this valuable study. I now know more and can share her valuable insights into what she calls "the trouble with play," something that had, for the most part, escaped my attention, although I've studied animal play for more than 50 years!

Marc Bekoff: Why did you decide to study dog-human play?

Julia B. Linares-Roake: I wanted to learn more about the relationships between people and the dogs that they live with, and how we can make our lives better for our dogs. The more I read on the topic, the more I wondered if our relationships with our dogs are always good for them, especially because dogs don’t really get to choose to live with us. We often control when they toilet, when they go outside, and who they see, and we can’t ignore the power imbalance there. I have my mentors to thank for helping me think this way, especially those I met through my work at the FIDO Lab at the University of Guelph, whose work is focused on making our lives with dogs better.

I often think about the work that you and Jessica Pierce have done around the ethics of animal companionship. You both highlight how we sometimes fail to see dogs in their dogness, like when we rush their walks or don’t let them sniff that extra pungent, yellowing grass. At the same time, I was also reading Afro Dog by Benedicte Boisseron, and other works that explored how things such as speciesism, racism, sexism, and ableism are all connected.

Donna Haraway is a feminist scholar who writes extensively about our responsibility to our dogs in her book, When Species Meet. She writes about how dog-human play can help us in our ethical responsibilities to our dogs, and this stuck with me. I wanted to explore how play could help us think differently about such ethical living. To do this, I used two approaches: (1) I took field notes about my own living and playing with my three dogs, and (2) I invited people to create multimedia stories (we call them digital stories) about play or joy with their dogs, in whatever way felt meaningful to them.

From these approaches, I created arts-based analyses (poetry, collage, soundscapes) which explore how people navigate the muddiness of living with their dogs, through play.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

JBL-R: I look at how play can help us grapple with both the possibilities and the challenges and inequalities that are involved in living with dogs. A lot of our daily routines–from leaving our dogs alone for long periods of time to controlling where they can and can’t go–are shaped by social norms that place humans first. Fields in the social sciences, such as gender studies, sociology, and interdisciplinary studies, can help us think about some of these issues.

One of my key messages is around defamiliarization. How can we step back from what we think “play” is supposed to look like and or supposed to do for our relationships with our dogs? For example, a lot of research talks about dog-human play in terms of object play (fetch, tug). But not every person or every dog can engage in this type of play, especially if one or both parties have mobility challenges. That doesn’t mean they don’t play or experience connection, but it does raise questions about how ableism might shape our ideas about what play can or cannot be.

From the dogs’ side, research from the United States suggests that many shelter dogs don’t choose to play with objects, and that dogs who don’t play with objects are less likely to be adopted. This has really serious consequences, especially if we consider dogs in kill shelters.

If we question our assumptions, we can also be curious about what play might look like. A great place to start is by using senses we humans rely on less often, though this doesn’t mean that we can think like our dogs or step into their paws. But we may think about our relationships with dogs (including play!) differently if we focus on what play smells or sounds like, for example.

Arts-based methods can help with all of this. Ultimately, though, I think play can help us think about the messy realities of living with dogs, and it can also help us not take ourselves too seriously.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

JBL-R: My work takes a critical social science approach to play, which means that I am looking at systematic pressures that influence our relationships (such as speciesism, sexism, and ableism, for example) with animal companions. I am particularly interested in what these things mean in our play with our dogs, and how families navigate these complexities.

There is wonderful work being done in dog-human play research, and my colleagues and I have a review of such work coming out soon. But I do believe that in addition to the work out there, we also need more research that considers the impact of socio-cultural forces, as they relate to the ways we talk about and actually play with our dogs. My work aims to offer one such avenue to do this.

MB: Are you hopeful that, as people learn more about dog-human play, they will broaden their horizons about the importance of learning more about this topic from unexpected points of view?

JBL-R: Yes, absolutely. I think of different approaches a bit like photos. We all have different perspectives, whether we live with dogs, train dogs, and or study dogs. I see each of these perspectives like a snapshot, where we can see some parts of a picture, but other pieces are left out of frame. If we can get snapshots from different angles, we might begin to piece together how we might ethically live and play with dogs, including how we can honour them in their dogness.1

Read the original article on Psychology Today →

item.title: When Your Child’s World Tilts
item.description:
Trauma

When Your Child’s World Tilts

Personal Perspective: Even if you’re distressed, you can be your child's anchor.

Posted March 11, 2026

Key points
  • When something frightening happens, children are watching their caregivers closely.
  • If we show them we are terrified, their terror amplifies.
  • There are concrete things you can do to project enough calm to anchor your child.

I was at the height of my career—flying home from New York City to attend an event at the United Nations about trauma in children—when my own world abruptly tilted.

Somewhere over the Midwest, my phone buzzed with a text from my husband: “[Our daughter] has little red spots on her legs.” I asked him to send me a picture. Tiny red dots scattered across her skin. As a psychologist who works with medical trauma, I knew this could be nothing—or something.

I landed late that night and peeked in on her as she was sleeping. She looked fine. I told myself I was being paranoid.

The next morning, I woke her up for school. As she sat up, my heart dropped. Overnight, those small red spots had multiplied, and now her arms and legs were covered in large, dark purple bruises. Her torso was mottled. Her skin looked like a map of something terrible.

Calling her pediatrician set off a chain reaction—stat blood work, rushing to the ER, doctors moving quickly but speaking in hushed, serious tones. Within hours, we had a diagnosis: immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), a rare bleeding disorder.

Her platelet count, they told us, was the lowest her pediatrician had seen in her entire career. Any small bump to her head, any internal injury, could result in what they candidly called a “catastrophic bleed.”

As a psychologist specializing in child trauma, I know that when something frightening happens, children are watching their caregivers closely. They’re not just listening to our words but scanning our faces, our breathing, our tone of voice. They’re asking, “Am I safe?” and “Are you okay enough to keep me safe?”

If we show them we are terrified, their terror amplifies. If we can act steady and grounded, even when we’re shaken, they feel more secure and contained.

Parents often ask me: “How can I help my child through something traumatic when I’m traumatized myself?”

You don’t have to be perfect. You don’t have to be unshakable. But there are concrete things you can do to project enough calm to anchor your child, even while your own insides are churning. Here are a few practical strategies that helped me that I now share with the families I work with.

1. Regulate your breathing (even if nothing else feels under control)

When something terrifying happens, your body does exactly what it’s wired to do: Your sympathetic nervous system flips on. Heart races, muscles tense, breathing becomes rapid and shallow. This fight-or-flight response is adaptive in true emergencies, but it also makes you feel more anxious, more flooded, and less able to think clearly.

Your child is reading that state in you.

One of the simplest, most powerful tools you have in those moments is your breath. When we emphasize our exhale over our inhale, breathing can help activate your body’s relaxation response (the parasympathetic nervous system), which slows your heart rate, steadies your thoughts, and softens your facial expressions and tone of voice, all of which your child will pick up on.

There are many different breathing scripts out there, but when you are in a panic, I find it’s best to go with simple. My go-to breathing mantra is “in through the nose, out through the mouth.” Because the breathing holes in our nose are smaller and more restricted than our mouth, this will help ensure we take in less oxygen, and emphasize our exhales.

2. Use healthy distraction—on purpose

When something frightening is happening, it can feel like you must constantly focus on it, as if vigilance will somehow keep your child safe. But neither you nor your child is built to stay in a state of high alert all the time. You both need breaks.

Distraction is not denial. It’s a way of giving your nervous system and your child’s nervous system short pockets of relief so you can come back to the hard stuff with more capacity. Some ideas:

  • Do the daily Wordle or a puzzle together. Let yourselves get absorbed, just for a few minutes, in something completely unrelated to doctors and diagnoses.
  • Swap silly stories from your day, or share light, age-appropriate “gossip.”
  • Watch a short, favorite show or a movie scene that always makes you both laugh.
  • Play “categories” (name animals, foods, superheroes) or a simple card game in the waiting room.

When my daughter and I were in and out of the hospital, we created tiny rituals of distraction: a particular snack we only ate after blood draws (crispy tuna bites), a game we only played in waiting rooms, a running joke about the hospital smells. These small, ordinary moments were lifelines. They reminded us that even in the scariest seasons, life still contained pockets of normalcy and even joy.

3. Protect your own basics: sleep, food, and movement

In crisis, parents often go into sacrifice mode: skipping meals, sleeping in chairs, ignoring their own physical needs. It’s understandable—and unsustainable.

Your brain and body cannot function well on adrenaline alone. When you’re sleep-deprived, underfed, and physically depleted, your emotional regulation plummets. You’re more likely to snap, cry, or freeze in front of your child. This is not because you’re a bad parent, but because your system is running on fumes. To the extent possible:

  • Eat regularly. It doesn’t have to be perfect nutrition; it just has to exist. Keep easy, portable snacks on hand (nuts, granola bars, cheese sticks, fruit).
  • Hydrate. Dehydration worsens fatigue and anxiety. Keep a water bottle nearby.
  • Sleep when you can. Trade off with another adult if possible. Even a short nap can improve your capacity to cope and to be present with your child.
  • Move your body. A short walk around the hospital corridors, a few stretches in a quiet corner, or standing up and rolling your shoulders can discharge some of the pent-up energy of stress.

It can help to reframe this: Taking care of your own basic needs is not selfish; it’s part of caring for your child. Your stability is one of your child’s most important sources of safety. Keeping your body supported protects that stability.

4. Reach out for your own support

Even when your child is the one in the hospital bed, you are also going through something potentially traumatic. Your fear doesn’t cancel out your child’s experience, and your child’s experience doesn’t cancel out yours—both matter.

Parents often tell me they feel they “should” be able to handle it alone, or that asking for help would take resources away from their child. In reality, getting support for yourself usually helps you be more present and effective for your child. Consider:

  • Emotional support. Call or text a trusted friend or family member and give yourself permission to be honest: “I’m terrified.” “I feel numb.” “I don’t know how to do this.” Being witnessed and held emotionally helps metabolize trauma.
  • Practical support. Let others bring meals, take care of siblings, handle logistics, or sit with your child while you shower or nap. Think of your support system as part of your child’s care team.
  • Professional support. A therapist—especially someone familiar with medical trauma or crisis—can be invaluable. You don’t have to wait until “after it’s all over.” Support during the crisis can reduce long-term traumatic impact for you and your child.
  • Peer support. If your child has a medical condition, there may be parent groups (online or in-person) where others truly understand the specific fears and rollercoaster you’re on.

It can feel vulnerable to say, “I need help.” But sometimes the bravest, most protective thing you can do for your child is to refuse to go through this alone.

When I look back on that season with my daughter (who is now, thankfully, stable), I don’t remember myself as perfectly calm or endlessly wise. I remember crying in my car, Googling too much, negotiating with the universe in the quiet of hospital hallways.

But I also remember sitting on her hospital bed, doing silly quizzes on my phone with her, singing Taylor Swift to distract from blood draws, and texting friends from the hallway so I could release my own fear before walking back into her room.

You don’t have to be a trauma expert to help your child through a frightening experience. You have to be a “good enough” anchor—a person who is trying, imperfectly, to steady themselves so they can steady their child.

Your child is not looking for a superhero. They’re looking for you: breathing, distracting, eating, sleeping, reaching out, and showing them moment by moment that even in the scariest times, they are not alone. The best part? Your child can emulate these skills to help themselves and others regulate, even when you're not around. Just ask my daughter, 7. She sang The Life of a Showgirl to our cat to calm him during his annual rabies vaccine.

Read the original article on Psychology Today →

item.title: "Schizophrenia": A Label Without a Disease
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

"Schizophrenia": A Label Without a Disease

Schizophrenia is a diagnosis that offers stigma, false certainty, and little else.

Posted March 11, 2026

Key points
  • Schizophrenia is a reified concept that does not provide useful information to patients.
  • Decades of study and billions of dollars have not clarified a disease process.
  • It is time to jettison the term in favor of a psychosis spectrum diagnosis.
Source: Edge2Edge Media / Unsplash

It is now over 100 years since Bleuler coined the term that would become a diagnosis carried by millions worldwide. It has become synonymous with "serious mental illness" and a grim prognosis of disability and social ostracism. And yet, we still know almost nothing about it. Despite billions of dollars of research funding, decades of study of the brains, the blood, and the genes of people with schizophrenia, we are no closer to understanding the pathophysiology of the "disease" than we were in Bleuler's day.

Imaging Studies: Lots of Money, Inconsistent Results

After several billion dollars spent on neuroimaging research, we have identified neuroanatomical differences in those diagnosed with schizophrenia, such as larger lateral ventricles, reduced dendritic spines, less white matter, and aberrant neuronal pruning. However, two significant problems undermine this research.

  1. Much of this research was conducted on people who were taking antipsychotics or with a history of antipsychotic treatment. Despite the obvious difficulty of disentangling medication effects from the effects of psychosis itself, researchers have concluded in several important longitudinal studies that antipsychotic treatment itself leads to reductions in brain tissue and enlarged lateral ventricles, independent of illness severity, substance use, and duration of illness (Ho et al., 2011).
  2. Brain imaging studies on young people at the earliest stages of psychosis also show brain changes, as do their unaffected siblings and parents. This data is cited as strong evidence of a biological illness. However, the studies don’t control for adverse childhood experiences or trauma, which also cause significant neurological changes, including reduced hippocampal and amygdala volumes, alterations in the anterior cingulate cortex, and changes in prefrontal cortex structure. Though not identical, these overlaps warrant investigating whether the brain changes seen in families of those with schizophrenia reflect shared trauma and adversity as much as—or more than—shared biology.

Biomarkers: A Red Herring

Over 30 years, promising biomarkers—BDNF, inflammatory markers, imaging and cognitive measures, and many others—have been lauded as the key to early detection and treatment. All failed to reliably distinguish those with schizophrenia from those with other diagnoses, or even from healthy controls (Abi-Dargham et al., 2023).

Genetics: Another Hopeful Direction, Another Dead End

The often-repeated heritability estimate for schizophrenia is 80%, implying that80% of the risk for developing schizophrenia is genetic. This statistic comes from twin studies conducted with identical and fraternal twins. These studies note that the concordance rate (where both twins have schizophrenia) of identical twins is approximately 33–50%, but only 7–10% for fraternal twins. The conclusion was that the difference in concordance rates determines the genetic heritability of the disorder, since identical twins share 100% of their genes, and fraternal twins share only 50%.

But the twin studies contain a major flaw: They assume that the parents of identical and fraternal twins treat their children the same way. Perhaps one doesn't need to be a child development expert to imagine that parents might treat identical twins more similarly than fraternal twins (who, in addition to not looking identical, may also be different genders). If this hypothesis is true, then in addition to shared genetics, the identical twins also share a more similar parental attitude and home environment, and perhaps, a more similar temperament since they share 100% of their genes. Since much of what shapes parental relationships with infants is the parent-infant temperament match (or mismatch), the identical twins are especially likely to share a more similar parental relationship. This conflation of shared genetics with more similar environment makes twin studies difficult to interpret.

Population-wide GWAS studies later found a far lower heritability estimate of 23–32%—meaning up to 77% of schizophrenia risk is environmental. And yet it is the flawed twin studies whose inflated figure is constantly quoted as proof of genetic underpinning.

Cognition in "Schizophrenia"

Schizophrenia is associated with significant cognitive deficits—attention, processing speed, executive functioning, working memory—often cited as proof of biological brain disorder. But abused and traumatized children show strikingly similar deficits that accrue over time. Since up to 80% of young people at high risk for psychosis report a history of childhood trauma, it becomes extremely difficult to disentangle trauma from "schizophrenia" effect. The cognitive profiles are similar in pattern, though slightly reduced in amplitude in trauma alone vs. schizophrenia—though one might expect that psychosis and trauma together would be more cognitively damaging than either alone.

Psychotherapy and "Cure"

If schizophrenia is a biological disease or cluster of diseases, it has proved remarkably difficult to pin down. It also fails to explain the long history of cure with intensive psychotherapy. Many psychoanalysts spent their careers treating and curing very ill patients of their "schizophrenia" (Karon VandenBos, 1981). With the demise of psychological theories for schizophrenia, there is no longer an effort to identify and address the psychological, temperamental, and familial issues that also frequently predate a psychotic diagnosis.

I work almost exclusively with patients with psychosis, many of whom have diagnoses of schizophrenia from previous providers. Cure for psychoanalysts goes beyond symptom remission. Instead it looks like growth. My patients go from being hospitalized on high doses of antipsychotics to extremely low doses or no antipsychotics, with no psychotic symptoms, the resumption of careers, new marriages, children, improvements in relationships with family, and increased personal coherence. How is it possible that sitting with a patient multiple times a week and helping them to reflect on their own minds can cure "schizophrenia" as it is currently biologically described? And yet, it can and it does. I have seen it in my practice many times, and it has been described in great detail for over a century. How do we integrate this information into our current understanding of schizophrenia? In my experience we don't. Scientists either insist the patient was misdiagnosed in the first place or doubt my description of therapeutic outcome. But what if these cures are real, and the diagnosis itself is illusory?

Conflation of Poor Outcome with Disease

Van Os and colleagues suggest that what we call "schizophrenia" is the poor outcome end of a psychosis spectrum (Guloksuz van Os, 2018). If we don't have a pathophysiological description of schizophrenia, nor any biomarkers or objective measures of disease course, then to ascribe those with poor outcomes to the diagnosis of schizophrenia, and those with good outcomes to the diagnosis of "something else," is to conflate poor outcome with a disease definition. It is a tautological argument where to have schizophrenia is to have a bad outcome and to have a bad outcome is to have schizophrenia.

Jettisoning the Reified Diagnosis of Schizophrenia

The term schizophrenia was coined over a century ago to describe what was almost certainly a heterogeneous amalgam of illnesses, from vitamin deficiencies to dissociative PTSD to syphilis to autism to bipolar disorder (Katschnig, 2018). Over time, we have siphoned off more clearly distinct illnesses, leaving a group of people with psychosis that persists, impairs functioning, and is not linked to a clear medical condition. We have called that schizophrenia and promised that the diagnosis will lead to better understandings of biological etiology, prognosis, and treatment. It has not done so and instead leads only to stigma and nihilistic prognosticating by providers. Let's say goodbye to schizophrenia and instead refer to a psychosis spectrum. Let's jettison this reified diagnosis in the hope of asking new questions, and once again being curious and hopeful about the meanings of psychosis.

Read the original article on Psychology Today →

item.title: Can Others Read Secret Messages in Your Body Language?
item.description:
Body Language

Can Others Read Secret Messages in Your Body Language?

Does your walking style, posture, and gestures, give you away?

Posted March 11, 2026

Key points
  • Although facial expressions are the best nonverbal channel to read emotions, body movements say a lot.
  • The way a person walks can tell others about their feelings, emotions, and even their personality.

Research in nonverbal communication has suggested that various body cues can reveal a lot about an individual. From your walking gait to gestures to posture, reading movement cues can tell a lot about a person. Here are some of the secret messages that body language can reveal.

Emotions in Body Movement

We look to nonverbal cues to decode a person’s emotions. The best way to detect another’s emotional state is to rely on their facial expressions. There is a great deal of research suggesting that our faces are a rich source of information about our felt emotions (or the emotions we are enacting to hide our true feelings). Think of the broad smile of a happy person, or the gritting and bared teeth of someone angry. However, what if you can’t clearly see another’s face? Can you, for example, read another’s emotions from a distance?

Research suggests that when angry, body movements tend to be stiffer, jerkier, and faster. When a person is sad, body movements tend to be slow, loose, and contracted—not at all expressive. Happiness, however, is characterized by expansive and loose body movements. For example, joy is associated with arm raising; grief is through downward-directed body movement. When fearful, people tend to engage in self-focused movements, such as hand-wringing or touching other parts of the body.

Through Gait

Can you identify a friend or family member, even at a great distance, by noticing their walk? Research suggests that we can tell a lot from gait. Not only do people have distinctive walking styles that are a personal “signature,” but emotions can be detected through a person's walk. Personality may also be expressed in the way that a person moves and walks. In one of our studies (Riggio and team, 1990), we found that the personality trait of extraversion could be detected from watching a person’s body language.

Posture

Our posture, the way we position our bodies, can tell a lot about a person’s feelings and intentions. For example, we can communicate interest in another person by orienting our bodies toward them—an open and welcoming posture. Or we can signal disinterest by turning away and closing off our body language. Pride or enhanced self-worth can also be conveyed via posture, with the chest thrust out, standing erect, head held high, while the posture of embarrassment or shame has the head downward and body slumping.

A review of research on how our body movements can be used to communicate is in a recent book chapter (Crawley and Riggio, 2025).

item.title: Reflecting on the Covid-19 Pandemic Years Later
item.description:
Coronavirus Disease 2019

Reflecting on the Covid-19 Pandemic Years Later

As a society, we have not fully processed the pandemic.

Posted March 11, 2026

Key points
  • The Covid-19 pandemic was a collective trauma.
  • More processing is needed to move through the trauma and its effects.

It was six years ago this week that the local government enacted the first shelter-in-place order in response to the Covid-19 pandemic. This was the beginning of the hunkered-down lifestyle: some working from home, some not. Lots of comfy clothes. Ordering everything for delivery. Canceling plans: travel, concerts, and eating out. Creating your Covid bubble of safe people to socialize with. Learning how to Zoom. Getting your school-age children to focus on their online classes.

At that time, we really did not know what we were in for. Setting politics aside completely, I think it is easy for people to forget that the reasons local authorities across the country enacted the shelter-in-place were threefold:

  • Covid-19 was a brand-new virus humans had never encountered before, and science and medicine needed time to study and understand it
  • In places like Milan, Italy, it was clear the virus strain at that time had the power to devastate or kill a large number of people (including otherwise healthy people) in a community, and the shelter-in- place effort was an attempt to save lives
  • Authorities did not want to overwhelm local health care systems

After all, each region only has so many hospital beds for the sick, no matter their illness (broken legs and heart attacks still happen year-round).

It is worth noting that local authorities announce shelter-in-place orders for other reasons, such as a gas leak or other emergencies. And so, we were asked, not required, to change our behavior immediately and dramatically in many industries and systems, like education, unprepared. It is understandable why so many people were angry and irritable during this time; the fear was palpable, and the guidance from experts was confusing and sometimes contradictory. This was especially difficult for those who have a high need for certainty, a low risk tolerance, a tendency towards rigidity, or a complex relationship with authority.

It is obvious in hindsight that because of the 2020 pandemic, we experienced a collective trauma. What were routine and mundane activities before Covid suddenly became fraught. What used to be reliable suddenly was not. In addition, other people, especially strangers, suddenly became potential huge and unknown health dangers. All of this was psychologically devastating to us humans, a social species that relies on others for connection, comfort, and survival.

As the world slowly and cautiously opened back up over the next few years (not without a few stops and starts), it seemed like everyone just wanted to go back to life as they knew it before, catch up on what they thought they missed out on, and not talk about or process what everyone went through. It was a “nothing to see here” mentality. This sent the experience and psychological effects underground.

As you read this and reflect on your personal experiences during the 2020 pandemic, ask yourself: Did Covid change you? If so, how? Besides the external factors like maybe you changed jobs, moved, or lost a loved one to Covid, I want to think about deeper experiences, such as your relationship to your family, your health, your priorities, other people, indoor and outdoor spaces, your sense of time, grief and loss, assessing risk, and seeking safety.

One thing I notice in my practice is that because of the 2020 pandemic, some people desire more time to stay at home and be by themselves (and with no shortage of ways to entertain themselves). More alarmingly, I also notice some people have lost some interpersonal skills as a result of the pandemic-induced physical isolation and psychological trauma of the experience. Things like having low tolerance for instability, frequent change, unpredictability, unreliability, ambiguity, social awkwardness, and vulnerability. I also see behaviors such as seeking predictability and reliability, like wanting some guarantee before taking a risk; poor conflict resolution skills; acting out when emotionally flooded; and emotional exhaustion from constant assessment of risks and safety in any given situation.

In the face of this, I see a need to build empathy, patience, humility, give someone the benefit of the doubt, and make eye contact. And most importantly of all, the internal motivation to build, or in some cases, rebuild, these skills. All of these together are a trauma response.

With all this going on psychologically and emotionally, it is no surprise that some people are increasingly turning to machines, not other humans, to meet their wants and needs. (Also interesting: using machines in our personal lives has simultaneously grown in the last few years.) When a person lacks the internal resources to deal with the complexities of human relationships, their wants and needs don’t go away. The person changes how they go about getting them met.

This actually means the need for psychotherapy, and especially psychotherapeutic groups, is needed more now than ever. In addition to processing the collective trauma of the 2020 pandemic, these are also places folks can build or rebuild their interpersonal skills.

In my own reflection on that time, I think of 2020 as the Year of Breath Awareness:

  • Covid-19 being a respiratory disease
  • George Floyd’s tragic and traumatizing final words: “I can’t breathe”
  • Then the country (and the world) collectively and metaphorically held its breath for the outcome of the presidential election that fall

Our awareness of breath was everywhere. Breath is a literal and metaphorical reminder of our vitality and its paradoxical fragility and strength. May we all take greater care of our collective fragility and strength.
